attempts.raw_response: The committee found that while the posts were "likely to cause offence" and could be considered "inappropriate in tone," they did not constitute a breach of the code because they expressed personal political opinions rather than representing official council policy. The report acknowledged that the comments had generated significant public concern and recommended that all councillors undergo additional training on social media use and the importance of maintaining public confidence. Mr Lloyd-Shogbesan welcomed the outcome and said he accepted the findings in full, apologising to anyone who had been upset by his remarks while maintaining that his intention had been to highlight what he saw as legitimate grievances. The council confirmed it would review its existing guidance on elected members' online activity in light of the case.

pair.human_continuation: Monitoring officer Anita Bradley, who wrote the report, recommended the council considers adopting a new policy for how councillors should use social media. Susan Brown, leader of the Labour group and the council, said: "This was disappointing behaviour for any councillor. "However, it is clear Ben himself realises that his actions were not appropriate and indeed referred himself for the investigation." Mr Lloyd-Shogbesan said: "I have never held anti-Semitic, homophobic or racist views and fully support the city council's position on equality, diversity and inclusion. "This has been a humbling and educational experience and I remain fully committed to serving the community of Oxford to the very best of my ability." Liberal Democrat group leader Andrew Gant said the posts were "abhorrent and unacceptable" and Mr Lloyd-Shogbesan should resign as a councillor.

A report has now said he "was not acting in a councillor capacity when posting on social media" and so had not broken the council's code of conduct.

source_document.title: Oxford Labour councillor cleared over 'anti-Semitic' Facebook post
